items.title: B cell-intrinsic TLR7 and TLR9 signatures define clinical phenotype and therapeutic response in lupus nephritis.
items.abstract: This study explores the expression of intracytoplasmic TLRs across diverse B cell subtypes in lupus, their association with renal activity, and their prognostic value. We compared TLR7, TLR9, and MyD88 expression across peripheral B cell subtypes by flow cytometry, along with 29 cytokines serum levels from 28 LN patients and 26 lupus patients with extrarenal activity (NLN). After induction therapy, TLRs/MyD88 expression was reanalysed according to treatment response in LN. LN patients were characterised by higher frequency of MyD88+ B cells (86.5% vs 52.65%, p 0.04), predominantly in transitional cells (97.7% vs 58.7%, p 0.03). Treatment-adjusted analysis revealed the association of TLR7⁺ naïve B cells (OR 1.02, p 0.01) and TLR9 mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) in transitional B cells (OR 1.008, p 0.004) with LN. The latter, together with eotaxin (OR 1.01, p 0.01), constitute the proposed LN association model (OR 1.006 and 1.01 p 0.01, respectively). At 6-month follow-up, the responder group showed persistently elevated expression of TLR7 and TLR9 in naïve and atypical B-cell subsets, including double-negative (DN) and age-associated B cells (ABCs). The association model for renal response included TLR7 MFI in naïve B cells (OR 1 p 0.05) and TLR9 MFI in ABCs (OR 1.001 p 0.03). In LN, increased MyD88 and TLR7/TLR9 expression in early B-cell stages may promote autoreactive cell survival and differentiation into autoantibody-secreting cells, contributing to immune complex deposition and eotaxin-sustained renal inflammation. In contrast, higher TLR9 in TLR7-dependent subsets may exert a regulatory effect that, alongside induction therapy, favours nephritis resolution.

items.title: Life-Threatening Pancytopenia and Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation Associated With Hydralazine-Induced Lupus and Vasculitis Overlap: A Comprehensive Case Report.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND This report presents a life-threatening case of pancytopenia and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) related to hydralazine-associated, drug-induced lupus and drug-induced anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (DIL/DIV) overlap syndrome. Diagnostic and therapeutic challenges are discussed. CASE REPORT A 52-year-old man presented with severe pancytopenia, fever, and possible pneumonia. He developed altered mental status, severe DIC with gastrointestinal bleeds requiring large amount of blood product transfusions, acute respiratory failure requiring intubation, acute kidney injury needing hemodialysis, acute liver injury, possible acute pancreatitis, and hypotension. Extensive investigations revealed no source of infection. Further workup was consistent with hydralazine-induced DIL/DIV overlap spectrum. Hydralazine was stopped. He was treated with steroids daily and intravenous cyclophosphamide every 2 weeks (7 doses). However, pancytopenia did not improve. Therefore, on the seventh day after the second cyclophosphamide dose, a repeat bone marrow biopsy was performed to guide further therapy. He later recovered, and hemodialysis was discontinued. A total of 104 units of blood products were transfused. After discharge, steroids were tapered off and mycophenolate mofetil was given for 2 years. In August 2026 (6 years after initial presentation), he was doing well, with normal complete blood count, stable renal function, and normal urinalysis. Array genotyping revealed NAT2 diplotype *5.002/*6.002, indicating slow acetylation (poor metabolizer status). CONCLUSIONS This case supports, rather than proves, hydralazine-induced DIL/DIV overlap as the leading explanation for life-threatening pancytopenia with overt DIC. It highlights diagnostic and therapeutic challenges and eventual recovery after hydralazine withdrawal and immunosuppressive treatment. Salient features include the detailed autoimmune workup, severe presentation, coexistence of pancytopenia and overt DIC, and extended follow-up within a rare clinical context.

items.title: Power Doppler signal and erosions underlie persistent tenderness in the absence of joint swelling following advanced therapy in established rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Persistent tender joints without concurrent swelling (tender only joints, TOJ) in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are usually attributed to pain states. However, this has not been systematically evaluated at the individual joint level. This study sought to evaluate whether TOJ respond to disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) at the individual joint level in people with RA and identify factors associated with persistent TOJ. In 200 consecutive patients with RA starting DMARD, tender and swollen joint counts (TJC/SJC), general health patient visual analogue scale (VAS), health assessment questionnaire (HAQ), ultrasound power Doppler (PD)), erosions (yes/no) and osteophytes (yes/no) of 26/DAS28 joints were obtained at baseline and weeks 12 and 24. Association between baseline variables and persistently TOJ at week 24 and TJC response (≥50% improvement) was determined. At least one TOJ was seen in 168/200 (84%) patients. Among all TOJ without baseline PD signal (533), 101 (18.9%) remained tender, compared to 32/107 (29.9%) baseline TOJ with PD. Baseline PD (OR 2.72 (95%CI 1.34-5.55), p = 0.006) and joint erosion (OR 3.77 (95%CI 1.58-0.03), p = 0.003) were significantly associated with persistent TOJ. HAQ was negatively associated with TJC response (OR 0.34 (95%CI 0.16-0.70), p < 0.01). Insufficient TJC response comprised an "osteophyte" group, a "high inflammatory" group and an intermediate osteophyte and inflammation but "high VAS" group. Most TOJ respond to DMARD. Persistent TOJ are associated with baseline PD signal and erosion, while HAQ associates with overall TJC response. Patients with persistent tender joints comprise sub-phenotypes requiring a nuanced understanding to inform therapeutic approaches strategies.

items.title: Mortality risk is associated with disease activity in patients with Sjögren disease: a South Australian retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: To evaluate the overall risk of mortality in Sjögren disease (SjD) and its relationship to baseline systemic disease activity in an Australian population. This retrospective cohort study included 241 patients fulfilling 2016 ACR-EULAR classification criteria from the South Australian (SA) Sjögren Disease Registry with up to 30 years of follow-up. Baseline data included patient demographics, serology and disease activity (ESSDAI). Analysis included the standardised mortality ratio (SMR) and cox regression. Patients were predominantly female (217, 89%), with a median age at diagnosis of 58 years. Most had oral (99%) and ocular (97%) dryness, Ro/La autoantibodies (193, 80%) and rheumatoid factor (RF, 142, 61%). ESSDAI scores were grouped into low (<5), n = 121 (50%); moderate (5-13), n = 92 (38%); and high (>13), n = 28 (12%). Mortality was not increased compared to the SA population (SMR 1.18, 95%CI 0.90, 1.54). Patients with high baseline ESSDAI disease activity had a four-fold mortality risk compared to patients with low disease activity (HR 3.9, 95%CI 1.7, 8.7). Moderate to high activity in ESSDAI renal or pulmonary domains, and any activity in the biological domain, contributed to this increased mortality. Rheumatoid factor positivity was independently associated with mortality risk (HR 2.2, 95%CI 1.0, 4.7). Causes of death were cardiovascular, pulmonary, infections, cancer, and kidney disease. High disease activity at baseline, including moderate to high activity in renal and pulmonary and any activity in biological domain, and positive rheumatoid factor are associated with increased mortality risk in SjD patients, underscoring the systemic impact of this disease.

items.title: Early Diagnosis and Therapeutic Evaluation of Rheumatoid Arthritis by a Mitochondria-Targeted Near-Infrared Fluorescent Probe.
items.abstract: As a chronic autoimmune inflammatory ailment, rheumatoid arthritis (RA) presents with persistent synovitis and progressive destruction of cartilage and bone structures, for which early diagnosis and real-time evaluation of therapeutic responses remain significant clinical challenges. Dysregulation of the inflammatory microenvironment, especially mitochondrial dysfunction accompanied by abnormal elevation of mitochondrial viscosity, is closely associated with RA progression. However, current imaging techniques are still insufficient for real-time visualization of these subcellular changes during disease development and treatment. Herein, we present a mitochondria-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe, YJ-1, constructed based on a donor-π-acceptor (D-π-A) framework for sensitive detection of viscosity variations and dynamic RA imaging. YJ-1 exhibits excellent selectivity toward viscosity changes, efficient mitochondrial localization, and a strong near-infrared emission at 764 nm, enabling high-contrast and low-background imaging. Moreover, the probe demonstrates outstanding photostability, low cytotoxicity, and good biocompatibility. Owing to these advantages, YJ-1 enables real-time visualization of mitochondrial viscosity changes in living cells, zebrafish, and mouse models. In addition, in a λ-carrageenan-induced inflammatory mouse model, YJ-1 successfully monitors disease-associated mitochondrial viscosity alterations and dynamically evaluates mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-mediated immunoregulatory therapy. Collectively, YJ-1 provides a robust imaging platform for exploring mitochondrial microenvironment dynamics during RA progression and offers a promising strategy for assessing therapeutic efficacy in inflammatory diseases.

items.title: [Medium- and long-term effectiveness of Swanson metacarpophalangeal joint arthroplasty for hand deformities secondary to rheumatoid arthritis].
items.abstract: To summarize the clinical experience of Swanson metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint arthroplasty for hand deformity in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, and to analyze its medium- and long-term effectiveness. A retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical data of 86 patients (243 joints) with rheumatoid arthritis who underwent Swanson MCP joint arthroplasty between January 2005 and December 2016 and met the selection criteria. There were 11 males and 75 females, with a mean age of 55.2 years (range, 37-75 years). The disease duration ranged from 9 to 26 years, with a mean of 17.97 years. The distribution of operated joints was as follows: 86 second MCP joints, 79 third MCP joints, 47 fourth MCP joints, and 31 fifth MCP joints. Preoperative Larsen grading revealed 59 joints at grade Ⅲ, 178 joints at grade Ⅳ, and 6 joints at grade Ⅴ. Clinical evaluations including the visual analogue scale (VAS) score for pain, MCP joint range of motion (active flexion, active extension, and total active motion), ulnar deviation angle, grip strength, and pinch strength were conducted preoperatively and at last follow-up. Anteroposterior hand X-ray films were obtained at the initial postoperative visit and last follow-up to measure metacarpal shortening, proximal phalangeal shortening, and prosthesis subsidence, as well as to identify prosthesis fracture. Postoperative complications were documented, and patient satisfaction was assessed using a questionnaire adapted from the study by Riches et al. All operations were completed uneventfully. All 86 patients were followed up 9-20 years with a mean of 14.89 months. At last follow-up, pain was markedly relieved in 77 patients, unchanged in 4 patients, and worsened in 5 patients. The VAS score was significantly lower than the preoperative value ( P <0.05). Significant improvements were observed in active MCP flexion, active extension, and ulnar deviation angle ( P <0.05), whereas no significant difference was found in total active motion, grip strength, or pinch strength ( P >0.05). Postoperative complications included 2 cases of wound infection and 2 cases of extensor tendon rupture, all were successfully managed conservatively, and no nerve injury occurred. Radiographically, prosthesis fracture was detected in 9 joints (3.7%), including 5 stem fractures and 4 body cracks. Mild periprosthetic osteolysis was identified around all implants. Ulnar deviation deformity recurred to varying degrees in all patients, and revision surgery was performed in 3 patients due to severe recurrent deformity, persistent pain, and concomitant prosthesis fracture. The satisfaction survey demonstrated a satisfaction rate of 94.2% for pain relief, 88.3% for hand appearance, 72.1% for finger mobility, 73.2% for hand function, and an overall satisfaction rate of 88.3%. Swanson MCP joint arthroplasty yields reliable pain relief and satisfactory correction of ulnar deviation deformity with high overall patient satisfaction in rheumatoid arthritis patients. items.title: Progressive morphological changes of a bioprosthetic mitral valve on serial chest CT preceding severe haemodynamic deterioration in systemic sclerosis: a case report.
items.abstract: Structural valve deterioration is an important cause of bioprosthetic valve dysfunction. Morphological abnormalities may precede clinically significant haemodynamic deterioration, but recognition of this progression may depend on longitudinal comparison of imaging studies. A 76-year-old man with a surgical bioprosthetic mitral valve implanted in 2014 was diagnosed with systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease in 2022 and subsequently underwent serial chest computed tomography (CT). Echocardiography in 2022 and March 2023 demonstrated preserved prosthetic valve haemodynamics. In August 2024, he was admitted with progressive heart failure and severe bioprosthetic mitral stenosis. Retrospective review of serial CT demonstrated progressive leaflet changes, from a relatively thin appearance in 2022 to mild thickening in 2023 and marked diffuse thickening with an apparent fusion-like configuration in May 2024. Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated severe leaflet thickening and restriction with a suspected superimposed thrombotic component. Despite therapeutic enoxaparin, recurrent pulmonary oedema prompted redo mitral valve replacement. Operative examination demonstrated diffuse leaflet thickening, rigidity, and commissural fusion, with non-dominant pannus and thin thrombotic material. This case illustrates the value of longitudinal comparison of existing imaging studies. Progressive morphological changes of a bioprosthetic valve were retrospectively identified on chest CT performed for a non-cardiac indication before severe haemodynamic deterioration was recognized by echocardiography. This does not support routine CT surveillance; rather, abnormalities encountered on existing extracardiac imaging may provide an additional signal to consider earlier cardiac reassessment.

items.title: Personalized Gout Education Using Large Language Models: Patient Acceptability and Short-Term Medication Adherence Outcomes.
items.abstract: Gout and hyperuricemia (HUA) require long-term management, yet patient education is often resource-heavy and generic. Large language models (LLMs) show promise in generating accessible health information, but their acceptability and behavioral impact remain unclear. This study evaluated the acceptability of LLM-generated education in gout/HUA and its short-term effects on disease knowledge and medication adherence. This two-phase exploratory study comprising a cross-sectional survey (Phase I) followed by a single-arm pre-post intervention study (Phase II). In Phase I, 184 patients rated acceptability of responses to 16 clinical questions, blinded to source: one guideline-based and three LLM-generated (Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking Experimental, DeepSeek R1, ChatGPT o3-mini-high). Multiple selections were allowed; mean selection rates were compared using paired t -tests with Bonferroni correction. In Phase II, 121 patients received personalized education from the highest-rated LLM. Disease knowledge and self-reported medication adherence were assessed at baseline and 1-month follow-up. Across 16 questions, all three LLMs outperformed the guideline in acceptability. Gemini demonstrated the highest mean selection rate (65.98%), followed by DeepSeek (56.30%), ChatGPT (42.17%), and the guideline (35.43%). All LLM responses were preferred over the guideline after correction for multiple comparisons. Among 105 participants completing 1-month follow-up in Phase II, knowledge of target serum urate levels increased from 23.81% to 97.14%, and recognition of asymptomatic treatment necessity increased from 44.76% to 83.81%. Mean medication-taking days increased from (18.26 ± 8.33) to (20.56 ± 10.67) days per month (mean difference 2.30 days; 95% CI 0.20-4.40; p = 0.035). LLM-generated patient education materials demonstrated high acceptability among patients with gout/HUA in the cross-sectional survey. In the single-arm intervention study, short-term improvements in disease knowledge and a small, uncontrolled increase in self-reported medication-taking were observed. LLM-based personalized education may represent a scalable adjunct to conventional chronic disease management strategies.

items.title: Mechanism-Guided Combination Pharmacology of Curcumin and Methotrexate: Translational Strategies in Cancer and Emerging Applications in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Methotrexate (MTX) remains a cornerstone therapy in oncology and, to a lesser extent, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), yet its clinical utility in both settings is constrained by dose-limiting toxicities, interpatient pharmacokinetic variability, and the development of therapeutic resistance. Curcumin (CU), a pleiotropic small molecule with well-characterized anti-inflammatory, redox-modulating, and chemosensitizing properties, has emerged as a potential adjunct capable of enhancing MTX efficacy while mitigating adverse effects. This review provides a mechanistically integrated evaluation of MTX-CU combination strategies, with primary emphasis on the extensive preclinical evidence generated in oncology. In parallel, we critically examine the more limited yet mechanistically consistent body of evidence in RA. Through this analysis, we examine how CU modulates key signaling networks implicated in MTX response and toxicity, including NF-κB, MAPK, STAT, Nrf 2 , and oxidative stress pathways, and how these interactions influence apoptosis, macrophage polarization, drug resistance, and organ-specific toxicities. Particular emphasis is placed on nanoenabled codelivery systems that synchronize intracellular drug exposure, enhance folate receptor-mediated targeting, and improve therapeutic index through controlled release and microenvironment-responsive mechanisms. Preclinical oncology studies provide the most developed evidence base for MTX-CU cotherapy, spanning multiple cancer models, mechanistic studies, and nanoenabled delivery systems. However, formal drug-interaction evidence remains limited and heterogeneous: only four of approximately 25 oncology studies performed combination index analysis, yielding condition-specific synergy, additivity, or mixed context-dependent responses. In contrast, RA evidence is restricted to four in vivo Freund's complete adjuvant studies and should be considered preliminary proof-of-concept. No published human trials have directly evaluated MTX-CU coadministration in cancer or RA. Accordingly, this review highlights key gaps in quantitative interaction analysis and PK-PD integration and proposes a translational framework incorporating biomarkers and precision nanomedicine. Overall, MTX-CU cotherapy remains a mechanistically supported but heterogeneous preclinical strategy, with the strongest rationale in oncology and RA representing an emerging application.

items.title: Spinal toxoplasmosis presents as myelitis in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus and immunosuppression: a case report.
items.abstract: Toxoplasmosis is a worldwide opportunistic infection that can be primary or latent, with reactivation in immunocompromised hosts. Spinal cord involvement is rare, reported almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised patients mainly those with HIV/AIDS. We describe a rare case of spinal toxoplasmosis presenting as myelitis in an adult with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in New Zealand. A 38-year-old woman with SLE, lupus nephritis and myocarditis, treated with hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil and recently increased prednisone, presented with right-sided sciatica progressing to rapid bilateral leg weakness. Investigations included contrast MRI of the spine and brain, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and T12 laminectomy with repeat biopsy for histology and PCR. MRI showed a ring-enhancing intramedullary T12 lesion with cord expansion and oedema to T8. CSF protein was elevated. Repeat biopsy revealed tachyzoites and PCR confirmed Toxoplasma gondii DNA, diagnosing necrotising toxoplasmosis myelitis. She received pyrimethamine, clindamycin and folinic acid with reduced immunosuppression. Follow-up MRI showed new basal ganglia lesions, prompting Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis, after which imaging stabilised. Six months later, her myocarditis progressed, and she died from cardiac arrest. Toxoplasmosis should be considered in immunosuppressed patients with myelopathy and intramedullary lesions. Early diagnosis, prophylaxis consideration and reduction of immunosuppression where feasible are critical to preventing irreversible neurological deficits.

items.title: Metallostasis remodeling in rheumatoid arthritis: focus on iron, copper, and zinc in the synovial microenvironment.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease characterized by chronic synovitis, pannus formation, and progressive bone erosion. Although cytokine-targeted therapies have substantially improved clinical outcomes, a subset of patients still experience inadequate responses, ongoing structural damage, and a sustained disease burden. Metallostasis contributes to immunometabolic and redox regulation and influences cellular functional states; its disruption is better understood as a mismatch between systemic redistribution and local synovial enrichment or depletion, rather than as a simple increase or decrease in total elemental abundance. In RA, iron dyshomeostasis is reflected by the coexistence of systemic iron restriction and local joint iron enrichment; copper dyshomeostasis involves acute-phase redistribution and lysyl oxidase (LOX)-mediated matrix remodeling; and zinc dyshomeostasis is associated with a low-zinc phenotype, altered zinc transport, and modulation of immune signaling thresholds. Through effects on redox regulation, immune signaling, and extracellular matrix remodeling, disturbances in metal homeostasis may contribute to persistent inflammation, synovial invasion, and bone destruction. In this narrative review, we discuss the evidence base, mechanisms of action, and translational potential of iron, copper, and zinc in RA. Moving beyond whether metal levels are increased or decreased toward their distribution within the synovial microenvironment, associated changes in cellular function, and experimentally defined causal links may open new directions for stratification biomarker development and precision intervention in RA.

items.title: A novel Germline JAK2 Splice-Site Variant Causing Exon 10 Skipping in a Patient with an ET-Like Thrombocytosis Phenotype and Early-Onset Tophaceous Gout.
items.abstract: Triple-negative essential thrombocythemia (ET) lacks canonical driver mutations, and its molecular basis remains largely undefined. A 26-year-old man presented with early-onset tophaceous gout and persistent thrombocytosis. Screening for JAK2 V617F, CALR and MPL was negative; extended sequencing identified a novel JAK2 splice-site variant (c.1326+2T>A), and RT-PCR confirmed complete exon 10 skipping, generating a truncated transcript predicted to retain the FERM domain-a configuration resembling recently reported germline JAK2 drivers of hereditary thrombocythemia.

items.title: Extracellular vesicles at the immunometabolic interface in rheumatoid arthritis: evidence, mechanistic boundaries and translational opportunities.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is sustained by reciprocal interactions among immune, stromal, vascular and tissue-remodeling cells within a hypoxic, oxidant-rich and nutrient-competitive synovial environment. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) can transfer RNAs, proteins, lipids and other bioactive cargo between these compartments, but the RA-EV literature often invokes immunometabolic reprogramming without directly measuring metabolism. We examine evidence linking EVs, immunometabolism and RA and distinguish direct metabolic effects from metabolism-linked mechanisms, context-dependent immune phenotypes and patient-derived biomarker observations. Among the endogenous studies examined, M1-macrophage EV-associated miR-155 provides a clear example in which recipient CD4 + T-cell metabolic function was measured, including extracellular acidification, oxygen consumption, lactate excretion and intracellular ATP levels. Most other endogenous studies identify metabolism-related cargo, signaling pathways or immune phenotypes without directly establishing recipient-cell metabolic reprogramming. An engineered plant vesicle formulation loaded with spermidine also altered macrophage extracellular acidification and oxygen consumption in experimental models. These findings should be distinguished from patient-derived EV associations and from engineered systems in which an exogenous drug or catalytic material may account for the principal effect. Direct measurements of recipient-cell metabolism remain uncommon in RA-EV research. Stronger studies will require well-described EV preparations, EV- and cargo-dependence controls, functional metabolic assays, physiologically plausible dosing and validation in primary human RA systems. In the future, these approaches could inform mechanism-based patient stratification, externally validated biomarkers and targeted EV-based delivery. These are research opportunities: patient-derived EV findings have not yet established a clinically useful test, and EV-based therapy has not established clinical efficacy in RA.

items.title: Hyperuricemia and Gout: Ancient Ailments' Advanced Approaches (A Narrative Review).
items.abstract: Hyperuricemia (HUA) and gout are evolving global health challenges, transitioning from localized joint pathologies to recognized systemic metabolic disorders. While traditionally associated with the appendicular skeleton, emerging evidence highlights a profound "extra-articular" burden affecting multiple organ systems. Although uric acid (UA) is often marked by its adverse effects, it exhibits significant physiological roles, including neuroprotective antioxidant properties. Comorbidities and systemic involvement are intertwined with HUA. Various factors contribute to the development of HUA, but there are options for reducing serum UA levels. The pathophysiology of HUA can be categorized into overproduction, underexcretion, and combined mechanisms, emphasizing that precision in subtyping is critical for optimizing pharmacological efficacy. Furthermore, this review analyzes the shifting paradigm in dietary management and the complexities of treating multi-system comorbidities related to HUA. We summarize the pathology and consequences of HUA and gout, alongside assessment strategies, investigations outline, differentials search, and evidence-based management protocols.

items.title: Association Between Anti-cyclic Citrullinated Protein Antibodies and Extra-articular Manifestations in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Anti-cyclic citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) and rheumatoid factor (RF) are established serological markers in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). However, their specific roles in the development of extra-articular manifestations (EAMs) remain a subject of debate. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate ACPA and RF titers and determine their predictive value for specific EAMs, particularly rheumatoid vasculitis (RV) and interstitial lung disease (ILD). This research was designed as a retrospective cross-sectional study. We analyzed clinical data from 205 patients with RA, categorized into an RA control group (n = 129) and an RA-EAM group (n = 76). Serum ACPA and RF titers were measured using a second-generation chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassay. To validate the findings, a post hoc power analysis was conducted. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated to determine optimal ACPA cutoff values for predicting RV and ILD. Serum ACPA titers, but not RF titers, were significantly elevated in patients with ILD and RV compared with those without EAMs ( P  < .01). To evaluate the diagnostic utility of serum ACPA titers, ROC curve analysis was performed. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis showed that ACPA had moderate discriminative ability for identifying RV (AUC = 0.755; 95% CI, 0.61-0.88). The optimal cutoff determined by Youden's index was 120 U/mL (sensitivity 90.0%, specificity 59.7%). For ILD, the AUC was 0.693 (95% CI, 0.59-0.78), with an optimal cutoff value of 42 U/mL (sensitivity 85.0%, specificity 46.5%). ACPA levels in patients with other EAMs did not differ significantly from controls. Our results demonstrated that serum ACPA levels were significantly higher in patients with RA-associated ILD and RV compared with those without systemic involvement. Notably, this association was not observed for RF titers. These findings suggest that high-titer ACPAs may serve as a more specific immunological marker for these severe complications than traditional RF. Not applicable.

items.title: Bilateral Sensorineural Hearing Loss as the Sentinel Presentation of Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis.
items.abstract: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a systemic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis classically involving the upper and lower respiratory tracts and kidneys. Timely diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion for the presenting symptoms. Otolaryngologic manifestations are commonly reported but most often involve the nasal and paranasal sinuses. Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) as the sole initial manifestation of GPA is uncommon and may contribute to diagnostic delay. We report a case of a 67-year-old male who presented with rapidly progressive bilateral SNHL that preceded pulmonary and renal manifestations by several months, during which the patient was treated for otitis externa and Eustachian tube dysfunction without improvement. Development of pulmonary symptoms prompted additional workup, which demonstrated markedly elevated cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA) and proteinase 3-anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (PR3-ANCA), raising concern for GPA. Histopathology then confirmed the diagnosis. The patient was treated with high-dose corticosteroids and rituximab with serologic remission; however, his hearing loss was largely irreversible. This case highlights bilateral SNHL as an uncommon sentinel manifestation of GPA and emphasizes the importance of considering GPA in patients with unexplained rapidly progressive bilateral SNHL. Early recognition and prompt treatment may reduce irreversible injury.

items.title: Minor Salivary Gland Biopsy in Sjögren Disease: From Diagnostic Criterion to Clinical Decision Tool.
items.abstract: Minor salivary gland biopsy (MSGB) remains an important tool in the evaluation of patients with suspected Sjögren disease (SjD), particularly when the clinical presentation and serologic findings are inconclusive. Although traditionally used to identify focal lymphocytic sialadenitis and determine a focus score, the potential clinical value of MSGB extends beyond a binary positive or negative result. Histopathologic findings may provide additional information about glandular inflammation, lymphoid organization, epithelial injury, fibrosis, and disease phenotype. MSGB may be particularly useful in anti-Sjögren syndrome-related antigen A/Ro (anti-SSA/Ro)-negative disease and may have a role in childhood-onset disease and the assessment of features associated with systemic disease and lymphoma risk. The procedure can generally be performed in an outpatient setting, although sensory complications should be discussed before biopsy. Salivary gland ultrasonography (SGUS) provides a complementary, noninvasive assessment of glandular structure and may help identify patients who require further tissue evaluation. This narrative review discusses the practical indications for MSGB, biopsy technique and safety, histopathologic interpretation, its role in anti-SSA/Ro-negative and childhood-onset disease, prognostic implications, relationship to SGUS, and emerging applications in tissue-based phenotyping and precision medicine.

items.title: Hematological Biomarkers and Disease Activity in Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study in Peruvian Patients.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disease in which accurate assessment of disease activity is essential for optimizing treatment strategies. Hematological indices derived from routine blood tests, such as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), have been proposed as accessible markers of systemic inflammation. To investigate the association between NLR, PLR, and SII and disease activity in patients with RA. A total of 188 patients with RA from a tertiary referral center in Peru were included. Disease activity was assessed using the Disease Activity Score in 28 joints with C-reactive protein (DAS28-CRP) and serum C-reactive protein (CRP). The Spearman correlation analyses were performed to examine associations between hematological indices and disease activity measures. Multivariable generalized linear models were used to determine independent associations after adjusting for potential confounders, including age, sex, disease duration, corticosteroid dose, and disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) therapy. Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, PLR, and SII showed significant positive correlations with DAS28-CRP ( r  = 0.66, r  = 0.47, and r  = 0.57, respectively) and CRP levels ( r  = 0.69, r  = 0.43, and r  = 0.62, respectively) (all P  < .001). In multivariable analyses, all 3 indices remained independently associated with both DAS28-CRP and CRP after adjustment for confounding variables (all P  < .001). Hematological indices such as NLR, PLR, and SII are significantly associated with disease activity in RA and may represent simple and cost-effective complementary biomarkers for disease monitoring, particularly in resource-limited settings like in Latin America. Retrospective cross-sectional study.

items.title: Relationship Between Serum Thyroid Autoantibody Titers and Disease Severity in Rheumatoid Arthritis Patients in Gonabad in 2022-2023.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease characterized by joint inflammation, pain, and impaired daily function. Rheumatoid arthritis can affect multiple systems, including the thyroid. Thyroid dysfunction may be a factor in the exacerbation of RA symptoms or the complication of treatment. The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between thyroid autoantibody titers and disease severity in patients with RA who were referred to the Allameh Bohlool Hospital in Gonabad. In this matched case-control study, patients were recruited during a 4-month period. A total of 182 participants were enrolled, including 91 patients with RA and 91 age- and sex-matched controls. Thyroid function tests (TSH, T 3 , T 4 ) and autoantibody titers (TRAb, anti-TPO, anti-TG) were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Disease activity was assessed by the Disease Activity Score based on 28 joints and C-reactive protein (DAS28-CRP) questionnaire. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 27.0 Statistical significance was set at P  < .05. Patients with RA demonstrated higher rates of thyroid dysfunction and autoantibody positivity compared with controls. In particular, more than 25.3% of patients with RA had hypothyroidism. This was significantly higher than in controls (12.1%). The severity of the disease, as assessed by DAS28-CRP, categorized the patients into remission (25.3%), low (28.6%), moderate (41.8%), and high (4.4%) activity groups. Elevated levels of TRAb, anti-TPO, and anti-TG were observed in 22%, 22%, and 19.8% of patients with RA, respectively. This compares to 9.9%, 15.4%, and 13.2% in controls. Elevated T 3 levels ( P  = .002) and TRAb positivity ( P  = .028) were significantly more frequent in patients with RA than in controls. Multiple logistic regression demonstrated that TSH (odds ratio [OR] = 3.498, CI = 1.279-9.570, P  = .015), T3 (OR = 4.057, CI = 1.526-10.789, P  = .005), and T 4 (OR = 0.105, CI = 0.019-0.572, P  = .009) were significantly associated with RA. Our findings suggest that thyroid dysfunction and thyroid autoantibodies are relatively common among patients with RA. These findings support consideration of thyroid function assessment in appropriate clinical settings, although larger prospective studies are warranted to confirm these observations.

items.title: Comparison of Adverse Event Incidence between Japanese and Non-Japanese: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis for Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, and Atrial Fibrillation/Venous Thromboembolism.
items.abstract: Enhancing diversity in clinical trial populations is increasingly important, particularly for underrepresented populations. We focused on adverse events (AEs) that have been reported to be more frequent in Japanese than in non-Japanese populations and assessed their plausibility. We conducted a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 24 multiregional clinical trials (MRCTs): 9 in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), 11 in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and 4 in atrial fibrillation (AF) or venous thromboembolism (VTE). Pooled estimates of the odds ratios (ORs) compared the incidence of targeted AEs between Japanese and non-Japanese participants using a random-effects model. For Janus kinase inhibitors in RA, the OR for the incidence of herpes zoster was 2.50 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.18-5.29, p = 0.0172), suggesting more frequent occurrence in Japanese participants than in non-Japanese participants. The incidence of pneumonia was statistically higher in Japanese in most COPD treatment groups and in the placebo group (OR 4.03 [95% CI: 1.33-12.19, p = 0.0135] for placebo). For direct oral anticoagulants for AF/VTE, the OR for major bleeding was 1.19 (95% CI: 0.91-1.56, p = 0.2105), with no statistically significant difference observed between Japanese and non-Japanese participants. This meta-analysis supported a higher incidence of herpes zoster in Japanese patients with RA, whereas the findings for pneumonia in COPD should be interpreted cautiously, and no statistically significant difference was observed for major bleeding in AF/VTE. Broader inclusion of Japanese participants in MRCTs may improve the interpretability of safety findings and the understanding of population-related differences in drug safety profiles.

items.title: A Case of Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome Presenting as Pulmonary Embolism and Renal Thrombosis: A Case Report and Literature Review.
items.abstract: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS), also known as Asherson's syndrome, is a rare and life-threatening condition that represents the most severe clinical manifestation of antiphospho lipid syndrome. Due to its rapid and aggressive course, CAPS is characterized by the development of widespread micro- and macrothrombosis, which results in multi-organ ischemia and failure. Antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune disorder, is characterized by thrombotic and/or obstet ric events, accompanied by persistent antiphospholipid antibodies. The case of a 36-year-old woman was described, who initially presented with low-effort dyspnea and abdominal pain, with subsequent imaging revealing pulmonary embolism and aortic thrombosis, alongside acute ischemic cerebellar infarcts. The eventual confirmation of a positive lupus anticoagulant solidified the diagnosis of CAPS. This case underscores the diagnostic challenge posed by CAPS, particularly when presenting with prominent pulmonary embolism, and highlights the critical need for prompt recognition and mul tidisciplinary management. Furthermore, the patient's positive outcome demonstrates the potential for recovery even in such severe presentations.   Cite this article as: Maradiaga FA, Diaz VS, Rubio MA, Arias JP, Alas-Pineda C. A case of catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome presenting as pulmonary embolism and renal thrombosis: a case report and literature review. Eur J Rheumatol. 2025, 12(4), 0018, doi:10.5152/eurjrheum.2025.25018.

items.title: Takayasu Arteritis with Neurological Manifestations: Clinical and Neurovascular Imaging Characteristics.
items.abstract: Takayasu arteritis (TA) is a large vessel vasculitis that may be accompanied by neurologi cal involvement in 57%-80% of the patients. The aim of this work is to describe the clinical and neuro vascular imaging abnormalities in TA patients with neurological manifestations. Thirty-nine TA patients with neurological manifestations and available brain magnetic reso nance imaging (MRI), MR angiography (MRA), and MR venography of the intracranial and cervical vessels were studied. Patients with thrombophilia or hyperlipidemia were excluded. The mean age at TA diagnosis was 30.56 ± 8.74 years, and 33 (84.62%) of the patients were women. The most frequent neurological manifestations included headaches (64.1%), syncope (12.8%), and visual loss (10.26%). According to the angiographic classification, 37 (94.9%) of the patients had involvement of branches from the aortic arch (Type I), and only 2 (5.1%) had diffuse aortic involve ment (Type V). Steno-occlusive lesions of the medium-sized intracranial arteries were observed in 11 (28.21%) of the patients. Features suggestive of small vessel disease were found among 16 (41%); 13 had abnormal MRI findings and 3 other patients had normal MRI and increased collateral circulation on MRA without associated intracranial arterial stenosis. Opening of the collateral circulation was seen in 14 (35.9%) patients. Venous involvement (affecting the cerebral venous sinuses and jugular veins) was found in 12 (30.77%) patients. Patients with TA and neurological manifestations exhibit a spectrum of extracranial and intracranial vascular abnormalities including large, medium, and small blood vessels, as well as the cerebral venous sinuses and jugular veins.   Cite this article as: Shahin AA, Zayed HS, Fathi S, Elsaid NY. Takayasu arteritis with neurological manifestations: clinical and neurovascular imaging characteristics. Eur J Rheumatol. 2025, 12(4), 0003, doi:10.5152/eurjrheum.2025.25003.

items.title: Adhering to European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology Standards: A Visual Representation of Nailfold Videocapillaroscopy Results for Systemic Sclerosis and Raynaud's Phenomenon.
items.abstract: This study aimed to create a simplified visual representation of nailfold videocapil laroscopy (NVC) results based on the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) standardization. The goal is to enhance the readability and communication of NVC findings among rheumatologists, other specialists, and patients. A diagrammatic representation was created using a free-form concept map to illustrate the capillaroscopic results based on EULAR standardization. Three different color-coded diagrams were proposed: a comprehensive and detailed diagram for research, a simplified version for clinical prac tice, and a minimalistic one for quick reports. The proposed visual diagrams effectively summarize capillaroscopic results, facilitating quick assessment. Testing with reference images from EULAR standardization demonstrated the practical application of this visual simplification. Capillaroscopy has many outputs. A visual diagram helps clarify their significance and easily tracks any changes. In this technical note, 3 different diagrams have been proposed; the first one is a comprehensive and detailed diagram suitable for research proposes, the second is simplified, suitable for clinical daily practice, and the third is minimalistic and convenient for quick reports. items.title: Focal Digital Clubbing as an Initial Symptom of Adolescent-Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Digital clubbing is typically linked to pulmonary or cardiovascular diseases. There have been no reported cases of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) where the initial complaint was solely foca digital clubbing and a chilblain-like rash on the ngers. A 13-year-old girl experienced digital clubbing for 3 months. Physical examination revealed focal digital clubbing of the thumb, index nger, and middle nger on her right hand, along with slight blotchy erythema assessed as a chilblain-like rash. Laboratory data showed hypocomplementemia and a high anti-double-stranded DNA antibody titer. She was also positive for antiphospholipid antibodies, had prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, and elevated anti-prothrombin antibody levels. She was diagnosed with SLE complicated by hypoprothrombinemia associated with lupus anticoagulant. Prednisolone treat ment resolved the digital clubbing and laboratory abnormalities. Digital clubbing may be an initial symptom of SLE. Screening for autoimmune diseases should be considered when a patient presents with digital clubbing not associated with pulmonary or cardiovascular diseases or malignant tumors.   Cite this article as: Sato M, Nagamori T, Kurisawa MJ, Tsuda J, Ishibazawa E, Takahashi S. Focal digital clubbing as an initial symptom of adolescent-onset systemic lupus erythematosus: a case report. Eur J Rheumatol. 2025, 12(4), 0075, doi:10.5152/eurjrheum.2025.24075.

items.title: Neuropathic Pain in Sjögren's Disease: Peripheral, Central, and Central Sensitization.
items.abstract: Neuropathic pain is an underrecognized extraglandular manifestation of Sjögren's syndrome. This article emphasizes 3 related, but distinct, pain domains: peripheral neuropathic pain, central pain, and central sensitization. Small-fiber neuropathy, distal axonal polyneuropathy, sensory ganglionopathy, trigeminal involvement, burning mouth symptoms, and corneal neuropathy all contribute to symptom burden. Ocular complaints may reflect either painful hypersensitivity or reduced corneal sensation with a neurotrophic keratitis-like phenotype. A practical framework that distinguishes peripheral nerve injury from central pain amplification may improve diagnosis, interpretation of symptom-sign discordance, and treatment selection.

items.title: Stromal Cells and Sjögren's Disease.
items.abstract: Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disease traditionally attributed to lymphocytic infiltration and epithelial dysfunction and destruction. Growing evidence indicates that stromal cells might also contribute to local glandular pathology. This article focuses on stromal cell biology and immunobiology where stromal cells establish structural tissue integrity, tissue niches, and a regulatory immune environment. We highlight new data establishing stromal cells as players in SjD glandular immunobiology and pathology where they promote local tertiary lymphoid structure development and inflammatory cell chemotaxis. Finally, we review the growing data supporting mesenchymal stromal cells as a cellular therapeutic to treat SjD.

items.title: Overview of the Use of Salivary Gland Ultrasonography in the Management of Sjögren's Disease.
items.abstract: This review examines the evolving role of salivary gland ultrasound in the diagnosis and management of Sjögren's disease. SGUS is a noninvasive, accessible imaging modality that detects glandular structural changes associated with inflammation, fibrosis, and atrophy. The article summarizes major scoring systems, including De Vita, Hocevar, and Outcome Measures in Rheumatology Clinical Trials, highlighting their diagnostic performance and increasing standardization. Evidence suggests SGUS enhances diagnostic accuracy when integrated with existing classification criteria, correlates with disease activity, and may help predict treatment response. The review also discusses SGUS applications in lymphoma evaluation.

items.title: Mouse Models of Systemic Manifestations in Sjögren's Disease.
items.abstract: Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disorder, yet research in mouse models has centered on glandular disease rather than the systemic manifestations driving morbidity and mortality. This article evaluates how well mouse models reproduce the systemic features of SjD, using the organ systems that define disease activity in patients as a benchmark. We focus on pulmonary and renal disease, where data are most developed. No single model captures the heterogeneity of SjD, so individual models may best represent distinct patient endotypes. Advancing the field will require systematically assessing existing models and building new ones for underrepresented manifestations.

items.title: Emerging Drugs.
items.abstract: Therapeutic development in Sjögren's disease has accelerated after decades of largely negative clinical trials. Improved patient selection, refined outcome measures, and targeted modulation of key immune pathways have produced positive late-stage studies and the prospect of disease-modifying treatment. This article examines emerging B-cell-directed therapies, neonatal Fc receptor inhibitors, costimulatory blockade, intracellular signaling inhibitors, immune-restorative approaches, repurposed therapies, and cellular treatments. It also considers lessons from contemporary trials, including phenotype-based enrollment, multidimensional endpoints, and organ-specific responses, and discusses how these advances may enable increasingly precise therapeutic selection.

items.title: Systemic Lupus and Other Autoimmune Disorders During Pregnancy.
items.abstract: Rheumatologic conditions occur in reproductive aged women, requiring a multidisciplinary approach to care. Patients require coordinated care with obstetrics, maternal fetal medicine, and rheumatology. Many drugs used for the care of rheumatologic conditions are safe in pregnancy, but detailed review should occur, ideally preconception, so the patient can be on the safest regimen while maintaining disease control. Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies particularly pose unique risks of neonatal lupus syndrome, including cardiac manifestations. Medical management is unique to each disease and includes ultrasounds and antenatal testing to optimize both maternal and fetal well-being and minimize perinatal risks.

items.title: Ultrasound screening and secukinumab intervention for subclinical and clinical psoriatic arthritis: a prospective real-world study.
items.abstract: This prospective real-world study primarily evaluated clinical and ultrasonographic outcomes after 24 weeks of secukinumab treatment in participants with subclinical or clinical psoriatic arthritis (PsA) identified through a risk-based musculoskeletal ultrasound screening pathway. A secondary descriptive objective was to characterize the screening pathway and the identification of ultrasound-detected subclinical PsA. Participants with psoriasis were enrolled at the Department of Dermatology, Tianjin Medical University, from September 1, 2022, to December 31, 2023. Participants considered at increased risk of PsA underwent musculoskeletal ultrasound assessment. They were classified as having subclinical PsA, clinical PsA, or no qualifying inflammatory ultrasound findings according to clinical and imaging findings. Participants who initiated secukinumab and completed 24 weeks of treatment and follow-up were included in the therapeutic outcome analysis. The primary outcome was the proportion achieving PASI100 at week 24. Secondary outcomes included PASI75/90 responses, ACR20/50/70 responses in clinical PsA, ultrasound changes, quality-of-life measures, and adverse events. Of 358 enrolled participants, 249 (69.6%) were classified as being at high risk of PsA based on the PEST score and/or prespecified clinical risk features. Among 194 high-risk participants who underwent musculoskeletal ultrasound screening, 159 had qualifying inflammatory ultrasound findings, leading to diagnoses of 42 with subclinical PsA and 117 with clinical PsA. A total of 38 participants completed a 24-week course of secukinumab. At week 24, 87.5% of subclinical PsA participants and 95.45% of clinical PsA participants achieved complete skin clearance (Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, PASI100). In the clinical PsA group, American College of Rheumatology (ACR) 20/50/70 response rates were 95.45%, 86.36%, and 72.73%, respectively. Ultrasound findings of synovitis and enthesitis improved descriptively in both groups. No serious adverse events were reported among the 38 treatment completers. In this exploratory, single-arm real-world cohort, a risk-based musculoskeletal ultrasound pathway identified participants with imaging positive for inflammatory synovio-entheseal involvement compatible with subclinical or clinical PsA. Among the small group who completed 24 weeks of secukinumab, substantial descriptive improvements in skin outcomes, clinical measures, and selected inflammatory ultrasound findings were observed. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound or demonstrate that secukinumab prevents progression from subclinical to clinical PsA. Key Points • In this exploratory cohort, a risk-based musculoskeletal ultrasound pathway identified imaging inflammatory abnormalities compatible with subclinical PsA in selected high-risk participants with psoriasis; the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound was not assessed. • Among 38 treatment completers who received secukinumab for dermatologic indications, high PASI75/90/100 and ACR20/50/70 response rates were observed at 24 weeks; given the single-arm, uncontrolled design, these responses cannot be attributed specifically to secukinumab. • Inflammatory ultrasound findings of synovitis and enthesitis improved descriptively in both groups, supporting ultrasound as a complementary tool for monitoring treatment response rather than as a stand-alone diagnostic tes. • Enthesitis most frequently involved the finger flexor and extensor tendons, the quadriceps tendon, and the Achilles tendon; isolated structural entheseal abnormalities (e.g., bone spurs and calcifications) were common and were not interpreted as active inflammation.

items.title: Prediction-aided tapering in rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with biOlogicals (PATIO): a randomised controlled trial.
items.abstract: This study aims to evaluate whether prediction-aided tapering of biological disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) reduces flare occurrence compared with disease activity-guided dose optimisation (DGDO) in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and sustained low disease activity. Prediction-aided tapering in rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with biOlogicals was a pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled superiority trial. Patients with RA receiving stable bDMARD therapy with stable-controlled disease, eligible for tapering, were randomised 1:1 to DGDO alone or DGDO supported by a previously validated dynamic prediction model estimating 3-monthly flare risk. Follow-up was 18 months. The primary outcome was the flare rate per patient. Secondary outcomes included any flare, major flares (> 12 weeks), disease activity score using 28 joint counts-C-reactive protein (DAS28-CRP) over time, mean bDMARD dose fraction, infections, and patient-reported outcomes. A total of 162 patients were included (81 per group). Over 18 months, the mean number of flares per patient was 1.00 (95% CI, 0.73-1.27) in the prediction-aided group and 0.73 (95% CI, 0.51-0.95) in the DGDO group (rate ratio, 1.32; 95% CI, 0.90-1.95). Any flare occurred in 57% of prediction-aided and 44% of DGDO patients, and major flares in 22% and 15%, respectively. DAS28-CRP trajectories, mean bDMARD dose reduction, patient-reported outcomes, and infection rates were similar between strategies. Nonadherence to tapering advice occurred in 23% of visits: 72% of these regarded advices to continue tapering, and 28% regarded advice to stop tapering or escalate medication. Prediction-aided bDMARD tapering using this model did not improve flare rates or medication use. Prediction models require sufficient and robust accuracy and prospective evaluation before implementation.

items.title: Relapse of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis With Kidney Involvement: A Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Relapses remain clinically important in ANCA-associated vasculitis with kidney involvement (AAV-KI). This study sought to characterize their patterns of occurrence, the factors associated with relapse, and the association of relapse with kidney outcomes. Retrospective multicenter cohort study. Adults with AAV-KI diagnosed between 2000 and 2025 in 7 French centers. A total of 460 patients were included. For the outcome of relapse, baseline clinical, biological, histological, and therapeutic variables, previously published relapse-risk scores, and biomarkers measured at 6, 12, and 24 months. For the outcomes of kidney failure and death, major relapse was modeled as a time-dependent exposure. First major relapse, relapse-event characteristics, kidney failure, and death. Cumulative incidence of relapse was estimated using competing-risk methods with death as a competing event. Cause-specific Cox models identified factors associated with the first major relapse. Landmark analyses assessed post-diagnosis factors associated with relapse. Relapse was modeled as a time-dependent exposure for the outcomes of kidney failure and death. Model discrimination was assessed using the C-index. Over a median follow-up of 62 months, 107 patients (23%) experienced 135 major relapses. The 10-year cumulative incidence of relapse was 31%, and the overall relapse rate was 48.6 per 1,000 patient-years. Relapses involved the kidney in 83 events (61%) and involved, at times, organs not affected at diagnosis. Relapse was associated with a higher risk of kidney failure (adjusted HR, 4.03; 95% CI, 2.03-8.00), but not with death. Higher eGFR at diagnosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) phenotype, ANCA positivity during follow-up, azathioprine maintenance, and kidney biopsy findings were associated with relapse, but their ability to discriminate between those who did and did not experience relapse was modest Existing relapse scores showed poor discrimination (C-index ≤0.56), and the best multivariable landmark model having a C-index of 0.71. Retrospective design, evolving treatment practices, residual confounding, and missing follow-up biomarker data. In AAV-KI, relapses are phenotype-dependent, frequently involve the kidney, and are strongly associated with subsequent kidney failure. Despite this, the ability to discriminate between patients who do and do not experience relapses remains insufficient. These findings suggest a potential role for dynamic risk models that incorporate longitudinal biomarkers and kidney measures.

items.title: Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis.
items.abstract: Dermatomyositis (DM) is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic proximal muscle weakness and distinct cutaneous manifestations. Skin involvement often precedes muscle involvement and includes pathognomonic features such as Gottron's papules and a heliotrope eruption. Pathogenesis consists of humoral immune responses and complement activation, ultimately resulting in vascular damage and myopathy. Notably, DM is strongly associated with malignancy, with approximately 20% of adult cases identified as paraneoplastic syndromes. There is a five- to seven-fold increased risk of malignancies, predominantly adenocarcinomas of the cervix, lung, ovaries, pancreas, bladder, and stomach, as well as non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Specific antibodies, such as anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP-2, are strongly associated with malignancy. Diagnosis requires careful clinical, histologic, and serologic evaluation. Cancer screening should be considered for all DM patients. Treatment can be challenging, particularly when paraneoplastic, as immunosuppression can exacerbate the malignancy. Managing the underlying cancer typically alleviates DM findings; however, refractory cases may necessitate adjunctive therapies (i.e., ACTH-gel or IVIG). Emerging treatments, such as Janus kinase inhibitors, have shown promising results for conventional therapy-resistant DM. Despite recent advances, paraneoplastic DM has been shown to have a worse prognosis. This further highlights the importance of detecting a paraneoplastic phenomenon early and adopting a multimodal treatment approach.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of upadacitinib in Takayasu arteritis (SELECT-TAK): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
items.abstract: For patients with Takayasu arteritis, a rare large-vessel vasculitis, there remains an unmet need for immunosuppressive treatments that reduce reliance on long-term glucocorticoids and maintain remission. This study aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of upadacitinib, an oral JAK inhibitor, for the treatment of Takayasu arteritis. SELECT-TAK is a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial conducted at 31 tertiary referral centres and university hospitals in six countries (Japan, China, South Korea, Argentina, Brazil, and Türkiye). Eligibility criteria included patients aged 18 years or older (aged ≥15 years in Japan) with Takayasu arteritis who had at least one unsuccessful attempt at glucocorticoid tapering, relapsed within 12 weeks of baseline, and were in remission with a stable glucocorticoid dose less than or equal to 1 mg/kg per day for at least 1 week before baseline. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to oral upadacitinib 15 mg or placebo once daily, with all patients following a glucocorticoid taper starting at week 4 (10% per week to at least 0·1 mg/kg per day). Treatment assignment was masked from investigators, patients, study site personnel, and study sponsor. The primary endpoint was the time to first relapse during the double-blind period, as defined by fulfilling the criteria of signs and symptoms in two of five categories (ie, objective systemic symptoms, subjective systemic symptoms, elevated inflammation markers, vascular signs and symptoms, or ischaemic symptoms) at two consecutive assessments or at one assessment when urgent treatment escalation was required. Efficacy and safety analyses included all patients who received at least one dose of the study drug. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04161898) and is active but not recruiting. Individuals with lived experience were not involved in the study design or implementation. Between March 3, 2020, and Dec 5, 2023, 59 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive upadacitinib (n=30) or placebo (n=29). The mean age was 38·2 years (SD 16·1), with most patients (35 [59%]) younger than 40 years. 53 (90%) patients were female and six (10%) were male. The majority of patients were Asian (44 [75%]), with the largest proportion being Japanese (36 [61%]). The primary endpoint was not met with upadacitinib (hazard ratio 0·52, 95% CI 0·24-1·12; log-rank test p=0·045). Median time to relapse was 107·9 weeks (95% CI 20·1-not estimable) with upadacitinib versus 20·1 weeks (12·0-127·1) with placebo. 11 (37%) relapse events occurred in 30 patients in the upadacitinib group and 18 (62%) occurred in 29 patients in the placebo group. Nine serious adverse events were reported with upadacitinib and four with placebo; no deaths were reported in either group. The primary endpoint was not met; the time to first relapse analysis numerically favoured upadacitinib over placebo, but did not meet the prespecified statistical significance threshold. No new clinically meaningful safety events were identified. Further exploration of upadacitinib in refractory Takayasu arteritis is warranted. AbbVie.

items.title: Chest CT manifestations of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis: A pathophysiologic approach and differential diagnosis.
items.abstract: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a rare form of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis characterized by asthma, peripheral blood eosinophilia, and systemic small-vessel inflammation. The lungs are among the most frequently involved organs, and chest computed tomography (CT) may also provide useful information during follow-up. However, the pulmonary manifestations of EGPA are highly variable and often overlap with those of other eosinophilic lung diseases. EGPA has historically progressed through three clinical phases: prodromal allergic, eosinophilic, and vasculitic. Moreover, clinical manifestations vary according to ANCA status. ANCA-positive patients exhibit vasculitic features, whereas ANCA-negative patients exhibit eosinophilic tissue infiltration, particularly in the lungs. This review summarizes the current understanding of thoracic CT manifestations in patients with EGPA. These findings were categorized into parenchymal abnormalities (transient ground-glass opacities, peripheral consolidations, and nodules), large airway abnormalities (bronchial wall thickening, bronchiectasis, and mucus plugging), and small airway abnormalities (mosaic attenuation and air trapping). Emphasis is placed on the clinical significance of airway-centred disease and its relationship to specific clinical phenotypes. Furthermore, this review summarizes major original studies of thoracic CT findings in EGPA and discusses the differential diagnosis of EGPA from other eosinophilic lung diseases, including chronic eosinophilic pneumonia and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. In conclusion, chest CT findings should always be interpreted in conjunction with clinical manifestations, laboratory data, and ANCA status. Familiarity with these characteristic imaging patterns and a multidisciplinary approach are essential for the early diagnosis and appropriate management of patients with eosinophilic lung disorders. items.title: The role of abnormal macrophage efferocytosis in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a classic autoimmune disease that ultimately causes multisystem inflammation and organ damage. SLE arises from a complex interplay of innate and adaptive immune dysregulation and loss of self-tolerance. Under normal conditions, apoptotic cells (ACs) are cleared by macrophages in a process known as efferocytosis. If this process is disrupted, it can lead to inflammation, developmental abnormalities, and neurodegenerative diseases. It is inferred that abnormal macrophage efferocytosis contributes to the development of SLE. This review summarizes the mechanism of efferocytosis and the effect of abnormal efferocytosis on the pathogenesis of SLE. Current evidence suggests that defective efferocytosis contributes to SLE pathogenesis, leading to the accumulation of uncleared ACs and subsequent abnormal immune responses. Thus, targeting efferocytosis may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for SLE. This review highlights the role of abnormal efferocytosis in SLE and discusses potential treatment of SLE.

items.title: Questionnaire-based nociplastic-like and neuropathic-like pain profiles in rheumatoid arthritis: a multicenter cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: Pain in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is traditionally interpreted as a consequence of inflammatory and structural mechanisms; however, neuropathic-like and nociplastic-like features may contribute to persistent symptoms and clinical heterogeneity. This study aimed to describe the distribution of questionnaire-based pain profiles and to characterize their clinical and symptomatic burden in patients with RA. A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted in rheumatology outpatients from two university hospitals in Spain. Patients with RA and chronic pain (> 3 months) were included. Four mutually exclusive profiles were defined using the Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI ≥ 40) and PainDETECT (≥ 19): nociceptive-predominant (both negative), nociplastic-like (CSI only), neuropathic-like (PainDETECT only) and mixed (both positive). Clinical variables included general pain, foot pain, Brief Pain Inventory severity and interference, Widespread Pain Index, and Symptom Severity Scale. Between-group comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn-Bonferroni tests. Of 111 patients analyzed, the nociceptive-predominant profile was the most frequent (43.2%; 95% CI 34.4-52.5), followed by mixed (31.5%; 23.6-40.7), nociplastic-like (17.1%; 11.2-25.2) and neuropathic-like (8.1%; 4.3-14.7) profiles. Overall, 56.8% (47.5-65.6) of patients showed neuropathic-like and/or nociplastic-like features. All pain and symptom variables differed between profiles (p < 0.001; ε 2 0.23-0.44), mainly mixed versus nociceptive-predominant. The mixed profile showed the highest clinical and symptomatic burden. Questionnaire-based pain profiling identified substantial heterogeneity in chronic pain among patients with RA. These screening-based profiles, not assessed against inflammatory disease activity, support a multidimensional assessment of pain in RA but do not establish distinct pain mechanisms. Key Points • More than half of patients with rheumatoid arthritis and chronic pain screened positive for neuropathic-like and/or nociplastic-like features on self-report questionnaires. • The mixed profile was associated with the highest burden of pain intensity, pain interference, widespread pain, associated symptoms, and foot pain. • Questionnaire-based pain profiling may help identify patients who could benefit from a multidimensional pain assessment, although its relationship with inflammatory disease activity remains to be established.

items.title: Clinical and Radiological Improvement Following a Switch to Upadacitinib in Giant Cell Arteritis with Recurrent Ischemic Strokes During High-Dose Glucocorticoid and Tocilizumab Treatment: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a systemic rheumatic disease that affects the large vessels. Although ischemic stroke is an uncommon complication of GCA, intracranial vasculitis may lead to recurrent strokes. An 81-year-old man presented with progressive gait disturbance. Physical examination revealed bilateral temporal artery tenderness with markedly diminished pulsation. His serum C-reactive protein level was elevated. Temporal artery ultrasonography demonstrated bilateral halo signs. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple acute strokes. Vessel wall imaging demonstrated circumferential wall thickening with contrast enhancement of the bilateral intracranial internal carotid and vertebral arteries. He fulfilled the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for GCA. Treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose glucocorticoid (GC) and weekly subcutaneous (SC) tocilizumab (TCZ) was initiated. However, recurrent ischemic strokes occurred early after treatment initiation, accompanied by progression of intracranial arterial stenosis. Therefore, TCZ was subsequently switched to upadacitinib (UPA) 15 mg/day. Following the switch to UPA, the serum C-reactive protein level normalized, no further ischemic strokes occurred, and follow-up contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated resolution of vascular wall enhancement. This case describes clinical and radiological improvement observed following the switch to UPA in rapidly progressive GCA with intracranial involvement.

items.title: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis complicated by anti-GBM nephritis: a clinicopathological case of PR3-ANCA-positive double-positive disease.
items.abstract: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) nephritis is an autoimmune disease characterized by rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, which is histologically defined by crescentic glomerulonephritis and linear immunoglobulin G (IgG) deposition. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is an anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and is strongly associated with proteinase 3 (PR3)-ANCA. The coexistence of anti-GBM nephritis and ANCA-associated vasculitis, termed "double-positive" disease, is increasingly recognized, although most cases are associated with myeloperoxidase-ANCA. A 77-year-old woman presented with fever, hearing loss, and renal dysfunction. Renal biopsy revealed crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG deposition, and serum anti-GBM antibodies were positive, consistent with anti-GBM nephritis. She was diagnosed with GPA based on refractory otitis media, PR3-ANCA positivity, and granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells on renal biopsy. The patient was treated with glucocorticoids, intravenous cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange (14 sessions), followed by avacopan. Renal function was preserved, and no progression to end-stage renal disease was observed at 10 months. We report a rare clinicopathological case of PR3-ANCA-positive double-positive disease with coexisting GPA and anti-GBM nephritis. This case highlights the characteristic clinicopathological features supporting the coexistence of these two diseases. The possible relationship between GPA and anti-GBM disease remains hypothetical and requires further investigation.

items.title: Lithium-associated polyarthralgia in rheumatoid arthritis following elevated C-reactive protein levels: A case report.
items.abstract: Lithium carbonate has multifaceted immunomodulatory effects. This report describes a case of joint symptom exacerbation in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) following oral lithium carbonate administration, in which an elevation in C-reactive protein (CRP) levels and an increase in neutrophil count preceded the onset of polyarthralgia. The patient was a 49-year-old woman in remission with normal CRP levels. After starting oral lithium carbonate for manic symptoms, an increase in neutrophil count and elevated CRP levels were observed within 7days. Only after the dose escalation, the patient complained of polyarthralgia with moderate disease activity. As lithium carbonate was gradually tapered, her joint symptoms improved progressively. Lithium carbonate therapy may exacerbate joint symptoms of RA. Elevated CRP levels were observed prior to lithium-associated polyarthralgia. CRP might serve as an early indicator of lithium-associated systemic inflammation and subsequent joint symptom exacerbation.

items.title: Complications of total hip arthroplasty in patients with ankylosing spondylitis: a meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder, with the hip being the most commonly involved joint. Total hip arthroplasty (THA) is the mainstay of treatment for degenerative arthritis of the hip. The purpose of the present study was to utilise a meta-analysis of the literature to investigate whether there is any difference in the incidence of complications after THA between patients with and without AS. Our hypothesis was that postoperative dislocation, periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), periprosthetic fracture and blood transfusion rates are similar for both ankylotic patients and patients without AS. PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane Controlled Register of Trials (CENTRAL) databases were searched for studies directly comparing directly postoperative dislocation, PJI, periprosthetic fracture and transfusion rates in THA, for patients with and without AS, between 01.01.2000 and 01.01.2025. The PRISMA guidelines were used to ensure transparent, complete, and accurate reporting of our meta-analysis. The quality of studies was assessed using the MINORS criteria. The random effects model was used for the meta-analysis. The initial search resulted in 864 papers. 95 duplicate articles were removed. Of the remaining articles, 4 were compatible with our inclusion criteria and were included in our study. The overall odds ratio (OR) of THA dislocation, periprosthetic fracture, PJI and blood transfusion in ankylotic patients compared to non-ankylotic patients was 1.63 (95% CI, 1.28-2.09; p  < 0.001), 1.62 (95% CI, 1.34-1.96; p  < 0.001), 2.35 (95% CI, 1.39-3.95; p  < 0.001) and 1.27 (95% CI, 0.79-2.05; p = 0.33) respectively. Our study suggests that ankylotic patients have a higher incidence of postoperative THA dislocation, periprosthetic fracture and PJI as opposed to non-ankylotic patients. No statistically significant difference was found regarding postoperative blood transfusion rate. Our study was registered on the PROSPERO platform and published online under the ID: CRD420250646593.
